In al-Kindī’s philosophical terminology, the “first cause” means God. See al-Kindī’s Treatise Explaining the Efficient Cause, in Al-Kindī’s Philosophical Treatises, edited and published by Muḥammad ʿAbd al-Hādī Abū Rīda, Cairo, 1950, vol. 1, p. 219. The term suggests a connection with Aristotle’s “first cause.” Al-Kindī also uses other philosophical terms for God, including “the First Truth,” “the true, first, complete agent,” “the Absolute,” and “the Eternal.” See Al-Kindī’s Treatise on First Philosophy and Al-Kindī’s Treatise on the True, First, Complete Agent, in the same source. The phrase “the true, first, complete agent” suggests the influence of the Neoplatonic theory of emanation. It points to a series of intermediaries in creation, each of which al-Kindī treats only figuratively as an agent—secondary and incomplete. God alone is the true, first, complete agent.↩︎

We can see this in his discussion of God through the concepts on which he built his complete theory of intellect and definitions, until he arrives at the concept of the “first cause” and the science devoted to it, which he calls “first philosophy” in keeping with the Aristotelian method. See the opening of Al-Kindī’s Treatise on First Philosophy, previously cited source.↩︎

One example, for now, is the basic assumption or proposition that “the universe was created from nothing.” Al-Kindī retained this proposition even though it conflicts with Aristotle’s theory of eternal matter, with the Neoplatonic theory of emanation, and also with Plato’s theory of Forms, as will become clear later.↩︎

In Aristotle this goes back to his well-known view that wisdom is the highest form of knowledge. For him, wisdom is the search for the causes and first principles of things (Aristotle, Metaphysics, 1, 981b 27). Wisdom holds this rank because it leads to knowledge of the highest principles—that is, the eternal principles. It is therefore knowledge suited above all to God rather than to other beings (Aristotle, 983a 9).↩︎

In the previously cited source, p. 182, al-Kindī says: “The first true act is the bringing of beings into existence from non-being. It is clear that this act belongs uniquely to God Most High, who is the end of every end. For bringing beings into existence from non-being belongs to no one else.” Here “bringing into existence” means causing something to exist; “being” means existence; “beings” means existents; and “from non-being” means from nothingness. The basic idea, then, is that bringing every kind of existence out of nothing is the first true act, and that this act belongs to God alone, because bringing existents into being from nothing is an act that no one but God can perform.↩︎

“Ideas” here does not have its modern meaning. The word is being used in an ontological sense, referring to existence. In this context, Plato’s “Ideas” do not mean a process by which knowledge is acquired, as the word might first suggest. They mean “special substances that exist independently of any act of knowing.” In this sense, Plato’s philosophy can rightly be classified as objective idealism.↩︎
Eidos is a term Plato used for the “Forms.” Other ancient philosophers used it in the sense of a model or pattern, as did some modern bourgeois philosophers such as Husserl.↩︎

We find an almost complete expression of these Platonic ideas in the dialogues where Plato explains his theory of beauty, especially Hippias Major (291d, 291e). In Timaeus (27d [= 27]) we also find an explicit distinction between what always exists—the “being” that does not undergo becoming—and what exists but is constantly becoming, meaning that its existence is changing and unstable.↩︎

The question of the oneness of God as “creator” receives a great deal of attention in al-Kindī’s philosophical treatises. See, for example, his discussion of unity and multiplicity in his first treatise (ed. Abū Rīda, vol. 1, pp. 132–141, 145), and his Treatise on the Oneness of God and the Finitude of the Body of the World (same source, vol. 1, p. 199).↩︎

In Arabic philosophical literature, Neoplatonism is called “the doctrine of the Alexandrians” because the school arose in Alexandria from the late first century BCE onward. Its influence continued into the period when Arabic philosophy began to develop.↩︎

Plotinus (205–270 CE) was the second of the two principal figures of Neoplatonism. The first was Philo of Alexandria (25 BCE–40 CE), but it was Plotinus in the third century CE who brought the school to its fullest and most complete philosophical form. The only primary source for Plotinus’s philosophy is the Enneads, in which Porphyry of Tyre collected, organized, and classified the writings of his teacher Plotinus into six groups of nine treatises each—hence the title Enneads, or “Nines.” By the time Greek philosophy was translated into Arabic, parts of the final three Enneads had already been translated into Syriac under the title The Theology of Aristotle. The Arabs translated them into Arabic under the same title. This produced the famous historical confusion in which these texts were taken to be works of Aristotle, leading Arab philosophers to mix some of Aristotle’s ideas with those of Neoplatonism. We now have an Arabic translation of several chapters of the Enneads, published by Dr. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān Badawī in Plotinus among the Arabs. In 1970, an Arabic translation of the Fourth Ennead, On the Soul, was published by Fuʾād Zakariyyā and revised by Muḥammad Salīm Sālim (Ministry of Culture, Egypt).↩︎
In Neoplatonism, the terms “emanation,” “outflow,” and “procession” are different words for the same idea and have the same meaning.↩︎

He gives another definition in his Treatise on the Definitions and Descriptions of Things (same source, p. 165): nature is “a principle of motion and rest after motion, and it is the first of the soul’s powers.” A further definition appears in his Treatise on the Nature of the Celestial Sphere (same source, vol. 2, p. 40), which also includes a definition of natural science: “The science of natural things is the science of things that move, because all of nature is that which God made a cause and a reason for the cause of all things that move and all things at rest after motion (...). Ays means existence, while lays here means non-existence. In al-Jurjānī’s Definitions, “identity” is explained as an expression for the absolute reality that contains all realities as a seed contains the tree, arising from the absolute unseen. Al-Kindī’s phrase therefore means that the thing came into existence from non-existence.↩︎

The phrase “the counting of the duration of what changes” means that motion measures the time of a changing thing. The Arabic word used here is an active participle from the verb “to count,” meaning to calculate or enumerate.↩︎

A thing’s inniyya means its reality or true nature. The word is formed from inna, the particle used at the beginning of a declarative sentence to affirm the reality of something. Inniyya is an abstract noun formed in the same way as “humanity” from “human” or “existentiality” from “existence.”↩︎
